questions.prompt: What is John Searle's Chinese room argument meant to show?

options.text: That running the right program is not, by itself, sufficient for understanding
That computers can never pass the Turing test
options.why_wrong: In the thought experiment the room is imagined to pass for a Chinese speaker.

options.text: That Chinese is harder to understand than English
options.why_wrong: The language is incidental; any language the person does not know would do.

options.text: That the brain is not a physical system
options.why_wrong: Searle holds that brains cause minds through their physical, biological powers.

questions.explanation: Searle imagines himself following a rulebook to answer Chinese questions without understanding Chinese. He argues that a computer running a program is in the same position: syntax alone does not give meaning.

sources.citation: Searle, J. R. (1980). Minds, brains, and programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 3(3), 417-457.
Cole, D. The Chinese room argument. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks about the Chinese room.
questions.text: In Searle's Chinese room, a person who does not understand Chinese follows a {{rulebook}} to manipulate symbols. Searle concludes that {{syntax}} alone is not enough for meaning.
questions.explanation: Searle argues that following symbol-manipulation rules, as a program does, does not by itself produce understanding.

sources.citation: Searle, J. R. (1980). Minds, brains, and programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 3(3), 417-457.

questions.prompt: What does Searle's Chinese room (1980) argue?

options.text: Computers will never pass the Turing test
options.why_wrong: The room passes for a native speaker; the argument grants behavioural success.

options.text: Running a program by manipulating symbols is not sufficient for understanding

options.why_wrong: Searle is a physicalist of a biological kind.

options.text: Chinese is harder for machines than other languages

questions.explanation: A person who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to produce answers indistinguishable from a native speaker's, yet understands nothing; the same, Searle argues, holds for any computer running the program. Syntax alone does not give semantics.

sources.citation: Searle, J. R. (1980). Minds, brains, and programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3), 417-424.

questions.prompt: What does the 'systems reply' to the Chinese room claim?

options.text: Embedding the program in a robot body would give it understanding
Simulating the actual neurons of a Chinese speaker would give understanding
options.why_wrong: That is the brain simulator reply.

options.text: Understanding is an illusion even in native speakers
options.why_wrong: That is not the systems reply.

options.text: The whole system, room, rulebook and person together, understands Chinese

questions.explanation: The reply grants that the person does not understand but locates understanding in the larger system. Searle answered that the person could memorise the rules and still understand nothing.

sources.citation: Searle, J. R. (1980). Minds, brains, and programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3), 417-424.

questions.prompt: In Searle's Chinese room, tap the part that plays the role of the computer program.

media.alt: A closed room with an input slot and an output slot, a person at a desk, a large book on the desk and boxes of symbol cards on the floor

questions.explanation: The person follows the rulebook's instructions to match symbols, as a processor runs a program; Searle argues that nobody in the room understands Chinese, so running the right program is not enough for understanding.

sources.citation: Searle, J. R. (1980). Minds, brains, and programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 3(3), 417-424.
